solution: Count the complement: strings of length n with no occurrence of P, then subtract from 2^n (and answer 0 when |P| > n). Track the set of pattern prefixes still alive as a bitmask A, where bit l means the last l characters match P[0..l-1]; appending '1' maps A to (A<<1)|1 and appending '0' maps A to ((A & starmask)<<1)|1, and a string is rejected as soon as bit m-1 would advance. That mask is exactly the Aho-Corasick state of the up to 2^15 concrete completions of P, so the reachable state count is bounded by the trie size, at most about 30*2^15; a dictionary-keyed DP over n <= 50 characters therefore runs in O(n * states) with states under 10^6. Measured worst case over adversarial patterns was 262144 states.
statement_summary: A pattern of at most thirty characters, each either a one or a wildcard and at least half of them ones, marks a binary string of length n as valid when some substring of the string matches the pattern position by position, with wildcards matching either bit. The task counts how many distinct valid strings of length n exist, where n is at most fifty.
notes: verify_insidersidentity.py checks both samples and matches the DP against brute-force enumeration of all 2^n strings for 500 random patterns plus edge shapes. aho-corasick is claimed because the alive-prefix bitmask is literally the Aho-Corasick state of the wildcard expansions (built lazily), which is also what bounds the state count; bitmask-dp covers the shift-and representation actually used.
